questions.question: Physical quantities are broadly divided into which two categories?
questions.explanation: The broadest classification of physical quantities is scalars and vectors. A scalar has magnitude only (mass, time, temperature); a vector has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force). Option A (base/derived) is a different classification — based on whether the quantity is fundamental or built from fundamentals. Option C is wrong — physical quantities are not classified by sign. Option D is not a standard classification.

questions.question: A unit vector has a magnitude of?
questions.explanation: A unit vector has a magnitude of exactly one and points in a specific direction. Its purpose is to specify direction without scaling. For example, î, ĵ, k̂ are unit vectors along the x, y, and z axes. To find the unit vector in any direction, you divide a vector by its magnitude: Â = A / |A|. Options A, C, and D are incorrect magnitudes.

questions.question: Given A = 2i + 3j + 4k and B = i + 4j + 5k, A + B is?
questions.explanation: Vector addition is done component-wise: A + B = (2+1)i + (3+4)j + (4+5)k = 3i + 7j + 9k. Option A is the result of subtraction, not addition. Option C has the wrong sign on the k-component. Option D is the component-wise product, not sum. Addition is the simplest operation on vectors — just add matching components.

questions.question: The dot product of two vectors produces?
questions.explanation: The dot product (scalar product) of two vectors produces a scalar — a single number with no direction. Example: work W = F · d is a scalar. Option A (vector) is the result of the cross product, not the dot product. Options B and C are wrong — the dot product of two vectors is a single number, not a tensor or matrix. The name 'scalar product' is a reminder of this.

questions.question: The cross product of two vectors produces what?
questions.explanation: The cross product (vector product) of two vectors produces a vector — perpendicular to the plane containing both original vectors. Its direction is given by the right-hand rule. Option A (scalar) is the dot product. Options C and D are wrong — the cross product is a vector in 3D, not a tensor or matrix. The magnitude is |A||B| sin θ and the direction is perpendicular to both A and B.

questions.question: The magnitude of A × B is?
questions.explanation: The magnitude of the cross product is |A × B| = |A||B| sin θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. Option A (with cos) is the magnitude of the dot product. Options C and D involve tan and cot, which do not describe the cross product. Note: this formula makes the cross product zero when the vectors are parallel (θ = 0 or 180°), and maximum when they are perpendicular (θ = 90°).

questions.question: For v<sup>2</sup> − u<sup>2</sup> = 2aS, the dimension of L.H.S is?
questions.explanation: v and u are velocities, each with dimension [LT−1]. Squaring gives [L2T−2]. So v2 − u2 has dimension [L2T−2]. This matches the R.H.S.: 2aS has dimension [LT−2] × [L] = [L2T−2], confirming dimensional homogeneity. Option A is velocity. Option B is acceleration. Option C is wrong — T should be squared, not just to the −1.

questions.question: For F<sub>1</sub> = (4i − 3j + 2k) N and F<sub>2</sub> = (−2i + 5j + 4k) N, the net force is?
questions.explanation: Vector addition is component-wise. Fnet = F1 + F2 = (4−2)i + (−3+5)j + (2+4)k = 2i + 2j + 6k N. Option A has the wrong sign on j. Option C has the wrong i-coefficient (4+2 = 6, not 4−2). Option D has the wrong sign on k. Always add matching components separately.

questions.question: For A = 2i + j − 3k and B = i − 2j + k, A × B is?
questions.explanation:
Using the determinant form:
| i j k |
| 2 1 −3 |
| 1 −2 1 |
i-component: (1)(1) − (−3)(−2) = 1 − 6 = −5.
j-component: −[(2)(1) − (−3)(1)] = −(2 + 3) = −5.
k-component: (2)(−2) − (1)(1) = −4 − 1 = −5.
So A × B = −5i − 5j − 5k. Option A has all wrong signs. Option B has the j-component sign wrong. Option D has the j-component sign wrong. The cross product is antisymmetric: B × A would give the positive of this result.

questions.question: In mechanics, the primary fundamental quantities are?
questions.explanation: In mechanics, the three primary fundamental quantities are Length (L), Mass (M), and Time (T). Everything mechanical — velocity, acceleration, force, work, power — can be derived from these three. Option B lists derived quantities. Option C lists fundamental quantities of electromagnetism, thermodynamics, and chemistry, not mechanics. Option D lists derived quantities (area = L², volume = L³, density = ML⁻³).

questions.question: Which system uses centimeter gram and second?
questions.explanation: The C.G.S. system uses centimetre, gram, second as its base units of length, mass, and time. Option A (F.P.S.) uses foot, pound, second. Option B (M.K.S.) uses metre, kilogram, second. Option D (S.I.) uses metre, kilogram, second plus four more (ampere, kelvin, mole, candela). C.G.S. is still used in some branches of physics for convenience, but S.I. is the international standard.

questions.question: The S.I. system consists of how many fundamental base units?
questions.explanation: The S.I. system has seven fundamental base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (electric current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount of substance), and candela (luminous intensity). This is the complete modern set. Options A, B, and D are all incorrect counts. Note: some older textbooks list six, excluding the mole or candela, but the current IUPAC/IUPAP standard is seven.

questions.question: The S.I. unit of length is?
questions.explanation: The S.I. base unit of length is the metre (m) — the distance light travels in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Option B (centimetre) is the C.G.S. base unit, a submultiple of the metre. Option C (foot) is the F.P.S. unit, used in the US and UK. Option D (inch) is a smaller imperial unit.

questions.question: The S.I. unit of mass is?
questions.explanation: The S.I. base unit of mass is the kilogram (kg) — historically the mass of a platinum-iridium prototype cylinder kept near Paris, now defined by the Planck constant. Option A (gram) is the C.G.S. base unit — one-thousandth of a kilogram. Option B (pound) is the F.P.S. unit. Option D (mole) is the S.I. unit of amount of substance, not mass.

questions.question: The dimension symbol for time is?
questions.explanation: The dimension symbol for time is [T]. Option A [L] is length. Option B [M] is mass. Option D [I] is electric current. In dimensional analysis, each fundamental quantity is represented by a capital letter inside square brackets, and every derived quantity is expressed as a product of these base dimensions raised to integer or fractional powers.

questions.question: The S.I. unit of electric current is?
questions.explanation: The S.I. base unit of electric current is the ampere (A) — one coulomb of charge per second. Option A (volt) is a derived unit — the potential difference that drives one ampere through one ohm. Option C (ohm) is derived — V/A. Option D (coulomb) is derived — A·s. Current is fundamental; voltage, resistance, and charge are all derived from it.

questions.question: The S.I. unit of temperature is?
questions.explanation: The S.I. base unit of temperature is the kelvin (K) — defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant. 0 K is absolute zero; the triple point of water is 273.16 K. Options A (Celsius) and B (Fahrenheit) are scale conventions, not S.I. base units. Option D (mole) is the unit for amount of substance. Note: a difference of 1 °C equals a difference of 1 K, which is why Celsius is often used alongside kelvin in practice.

questions.question: The S.I. unit of luminous intensity is?
questions.explanation: The S.I. base unit of luminous intensity is the candela (cd) — the luminous power emitted by a source in a particular direction per steradian. Option A (mole) is amount of substance. Option B (kelvin) is temperature. Option D (ampere) is electric current. The candela is the least intuitive of the seven S.I. base units because it depends on human eye sensitivity, not just physical power.

questions.question: A dimensional formula shows how derived quantities depend on what?
questions.explanation: A dimensional formula expresses a derived quantity as a product of base dimensions (M, L, T, I, Θ, N, J) raised to particular powers. For example, velocity has dimensional formula [LT−1] — length to the first power, time to the negative first power. Options B, C, and D describe quantities themselves, not what a dimensional formula shows. Dimensional formulas say nothing about magnitude, direction, or numerical constants.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of velocity is?
questions.explanation: Velocity = displacement / time. Dimension of displacement is [L], of time is [T]. So [LT−1]. Option B is [LT−2] — acceleration (velocity per unit time). Option C is [L2T−2] — same as energy per unit mass (v²). Option D is [MLT−2] — force.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of acceleration is?
questions.explanation: Acceleration = change in velocity / time. Velocity has [LT−1], divided by time [T] gives [LT−2]. Option A is velocity itself. Option C is force (mass × acceleration). Option D is the same dimension as v² (energy per unit mass), commonly used in the equation v² = 2as.

questions.question: From Newton's second law, the dimension of force is?
questions.explanation: Newton's second law: F = ma. Mass has [M], acceleration has [LT−2]. Multiplying gives [MLT−2]. This is the dimension of every force — weight, tension, friction, gravitational force, etc. Option B is work/energy. Option C is pressure/stress/modulus of elasticity. Option D is power.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of pressure is?
questions.explanation: Pressure = force / area. Force has [MLT−2], area has [L2]. Dividing gives [ML−1T−2]. Option A is force itself. Option C is work/energy. Option D is power. Stress and modulus of elasticity share this same dimension as pressure.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of work or energy is?
questions.explanation: Work = force × distance. Force has [MLT−2], distance has [L]. Multiplying gives [ML2T−2]. This dimension is shared by work, kinetic energy, potential energy, heat, torque (in some conventions), and any form of energy. Option A is force. Option C is power. Option D is pressure.

questions.question: The dimensional formula of power is?
questions.explanation: Power = work / time. Work has [ML2T−2], divided by time [T] gives [ML2T−3]. Option A is work/energy. Option C is force. Option D is the dimension of coefficient of viscosity. The watt (W) — one joule per second — is the S.I. unit of power.

questions.question: Modulus of elasticity has the same dimension as what?
questions.explanation: Modulus of elasticity (Young's modulus, bulk modulus, shear modulus) is defined as stress / strain. Strain is dimensionless (length / length). So the dimension of modulus of elasticity equals the dimension of stress — [ML−1T−2]. Option A (strain) is dimensionless. Option C (force) is [MLT−2]. Option D (work) is [ML2T−2].

questions.question: The dimensional formula of coefficient of viscosity is?
questions.explanation: Coefficient of viscosity η relates shear stress to velocity gradient: F = η A (dv/dx). Solving for η: η = F / (A · dv/dx). Force [MLT−2] ÷ (area [L2] × velocity gradient [T−1]) gives [ML−1T−1]. Option B is force. Option C is work. Option D is pressure.

questions.question: Dimensional equations are used to check what?
questions.explanation: The primary use of dimensional equations is to check homogeneity — whether the equation is dimensionally balanced. Every term on the left side of a physically valid equation must have the same dimension as every term on the right side. Options A, B, and D describe physical properties that dimensional analysis does not check — dimensional analysis is blind to temperature, direction, and magnitude.

questions.question: In dimensional homogeneity, L.H.S dimensions must equal what?
questions.explanation: The principle of dimensional homogeneity states that for any valid physical equation, the dimensions on the left-hand side (L.H.S) must equal the dimensions on the right-hand side (R.H.S). This is the bedrock of dimensional analysis. Option A is wrong because numerical constants (like 2 or ½) are dimensionless. Options B and C are irrelevant — dimensions ignore direction and units prefixes.

questions.question: The S.I. unit of coefficient of viscosity is?
questions.explanation: The dimension of coefficient of viscosity is [ML−1T−1], so the S.I. unit is kg m−1 s−1 — also written as Pa·s (pascal-second) or N·s/m². Options A, B, and C have incorrect exponents. Option A is the dimension of force. Option B is work/energy. Option C is pressure. The correct unit is essential when solving problems involving viscosity of fluids.
